extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in international and political news
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and assembling newspaper-style international news dispatches: concise datelined leads, agency attribution, official statements, background context, and follow-up paragraphs across multiple related stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and source attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Include location, date and news agency at the top of the piece (dateline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: 'Bucharest, Romania, Tuesday, Oct. AP)' and multiple datelined leads (e.g., 'Canton, OCT. 3—CAP)—SOVIET RECOGNITION...'). Use agency labels (AP, CAP) and city/date to orient the reader immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (lede) states the most newsworthy fact immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a concise first sentence or paragraph that summarizes the core development or claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown verbatim: 'The official news agency Agerpres announced today that Romania has recognized the new Chinese Communist government.' The lead should put the main event up front so readers know the story's significance at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute claims to named officials or agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Report significant assertions and decisions by attributing them to the appropriate person, office, or agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page attributes actions and quotes (e.g., 'Foreign Minister anie Pauker had telegraphed Chou En-Lai', 'The agency said...'). Use named sources (minister, agency) rather than unsigned assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include direct quotations and paraphrase for official reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quoted language and paraphrase to convey how officials and governments describe events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mrs. Pauker hailed the “new China” as an active factor...' and other quoted phrases. Quotes convey tone and explicit positions; paraphrase can summarize longer statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate the current event with prior relevant facts, treaties, timelines, and earlier decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references prior events (e.g., 'The wartime Romanian Government... broke off relations with Nationalist China in June, 1941', 'Soviet Union announced Sunday, its recognition...'). Background helps readers understand implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report multiple sides and conflicting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Present competing narratives, accusations, protests or denials from the parties involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: 'The Foreign Ministry charged that Yugoslavia has not fulfilled the border agreement', 'Yugoslavia retaliated by expelling nine Hungarians.' The story lists charges, countercharges and denouncements so readers see differing positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific factual details (names, numbers, dates, places)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include concrete details—personal names, numeric figures, dates, precise locations—to ground the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page examples: 'more than 1,200 Greek children', 'Kukong, 125 miles northeast', '550' (casualties), 'Oct. 3'. Specifics increase credibility and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover institutional processes and vote outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on international bodies, detail resolutions, committee actions, membership and vote tallies and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: explanation of U.N. committee actions: 'The vote... was passed by an overwhelming 44 to six, with five abstentions.' Describe mandates (e.g., expanded duties to observe military threats) and next steps (plenary approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-location, multi-dispatch structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble short datelined dispatches from several cities or correspondents into one page/packet to cover related developments across regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contains dispatches from Bucharest, Canton, Tokyo, Prague, Lake Success, Berlin, Belgrade, etc. Editors can group them under thematic headings to give a broad picture of a developing international story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest or illustrative vignettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement policy/diplomatic coverage with individual-level stories or anecdotes that illustrate broader themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a personal profile appears—'MASAYOSHI KAWATSU, 20... wants to become an international Garry Davis'—which humanizes postwar concerns and ideals amid geopolitical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral, objective tone with journalistic brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a factual, non-editorial voice, favoring short paragraphs and straightforward phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copy follows AP-style concise sentences and neutral reporting; paragraphs are short and focused on single facts or claims to ease scanning and avoid editorializing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence details: expand from lead into corroboration and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: After the lede, supply corroborating facts, reactions, implications, and related developments in descending importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern on page: lead → supporting details and quotes → background history → related international ramifications (e.g., diplomatic break-offs, allied reactions). This inverted-pyramid sequencing helps editors trim from the bottom if needed.
